clue.text: “Lethal head-shrinker gangs run amok” (Standard, Dec)

indicators.note: to run amok is to rampage wildly, so the letters break loose from their order

blocks.note: all twenty-three letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A tabloid-style headline about murderous gangs of tribal head-shrinkers, credited to the Standard newspaper in December.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like a newspaper credit, but it is the definition: a standard is a well-known song, and Dec says when this one is sung. The answer is HARK THE HERALD ANGELS SING.
explanation.definitionFit: This carol is a perennial favourite sung every year in the run-up to Christmas, so it counts as a December evergreen song.

clue.text: I glance nervously like one on top of tree?

definitions.text: like one on top of tree?

indicators.note: something done nervously is jittery and unsettled, so the letters are shaken up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone perched at the top of a tree looks down anxiously.
explanation.walkthrough: The tree is a Christmas tree, and the figure traditionally placed on top of it is an angel, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: An angel often crowns a Christmas tree, and the adjective describes resembling that heavenly figure.

clue.text: Understand only half of what’s said

indicators.note: keeping only half a word means the other half is thrown away

blocks.note: what is said is what is spoken

explanation.surface: A listener catches only part of a conversation and admits to following just half of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a listener catching half a conversation; the half kept is the back three letters of SPOKEN, giving KEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ken is a Scottish and northern dialect verb meaning to know or recognise, also familiar from the noun phrase beyond one's ken.

clue.text: Buddy plant

definitions.note: Buddy is a first name; the answer is the surname that goes with it

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of the bespectacled 1950s American rock and roll singer who recorded Peggy Sue
second meaning: the evergreen shrub with spiky leaves and red berries

explanation.walkthrough: Buddy looks like a friend, but it is the first name of the singer; the plant is the one used in Christmas decorations.
explanation.definitionFit: The rock star's surname and the prickly evergreen shrub with scarlet berries share the same spelling.

clue.text: Old hat picked up by grass for Christmas?

indicators.note: whatever is picked up is gathered into the grasp of something else, so it ends up inside

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
lid is slang for a hat
hay is dried grass

explanation.surface: A worn-out hat is found lying in the grass at Christmas time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old hat' looks like a single phrase meaning unoriginal, but it splits into two pieces that sit inside HAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas is one example of a public day off work, which the question mark flags as an instance rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Fancy arts fair attended by a religious type

indicators.note: fancy means ornate or elaborate, so the letters are dressed up into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A smart arts fair draws a devout visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as an adjective for the fair, but it is the signal; the lone 'a' joins the fodder to supply the third A.
explanation.definitionFit: A Rastafari is a follower of the Jamaican faith that reveres Haile Selassie, so the word names a devout believer.

clue.text: Extras ask for stories Spooner narrates

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words when he spoke

blocks.note: to ask for is to beg; it lends its opening sound to the second word and takes that word's in exchange
stories are lies, as in telling stories; its first sound swaps with the first word's

explanation.surface: Film extras plead for tales that the narrator then tells.
explanation.walkthrough: Extras looks like film walk-ons, but these are cricket runs. A leg bye is a run scored when the ball comes off the batter's body rather than the bat.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, extras are runs not credited to a batter, and leg byes are one of the standard kinds.

clue.text: Tune a Wagnerian may put in a new arrangement

indicators.note: a new arrangement of a piece is a rearrangement, so the letters take a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An opera fan of Wagner might rework a melody into a fresh musical arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all about musical arrangements, which hides that 'arrangement' is the letter signal; 'may' belongs in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a well-loved children's Christmas carol, so it is a song melody in the plainest sense.

clue.text: A Fish Called Wanda essentially left out on reflection

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letter is wanted
anything left out is omitted, so those letters are taken away
a reflection shows things back to front, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: to call someone on the phone is to ring them; past tense rang
the central letter of the name

explanation.surface: Looks like a comment on the film A Fish Called Wanda.
explanation.walkthrough: The film title splits across the clue: 'A Fish' is the definition and 'Called' starts the wordplay. Removing the N from RANG leaves RAG.
explanation.definitionFit: The gar is a long-snouted freshwater fish of North America, often called a garfish.

clue.text: For example, wife wearing king’s stockings?

blocks.note: EG is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for example
W is the abbreviation for wife
Lear is Shakespeare's tragic king

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing' suggests clothes, but here it means sitting inside: the abbreviations go inside the king's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockings are one example of clothing for the lower limbs, and the question mark marks them as an instance.

clue.text: Piece of music in the style of 4’33” that follows vespers

vespers is the evening service, after which darkness comes

explanation.surface: A composition modelled on John Cage's notorious piece is played after evening prayers.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are mini definitions: the Cage piece is soundless, and evening prayer leads into the dark hours.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the famous German Christmas carol Stille Nacht, so it is a well-known musical work.

clue.text: Help, or not, to sort out sacked worker’s home

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacked' looks like fired, but the worker carries a sack: it is Father Christmas, delivering presents.
explanation.definitionFit: Santa Claus is said to live and run his toy workshop at the top of the world, near the Arctic.

clue.text: A knight captivated by end of awful pain

indicators.note: a captive is held inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: taken as written

a goal is an aim or end

explanation.walkthrough: 'End of awful' looks like a request for the letter L, but 'end' is a synonym and 'of awful pain' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to agony, especially the intense suffering of death throes.

clue.text: Drop in network, second for satellite dish

asking for the second means picking out the letter in position two

the letter in position two of the word

clue.text: They often patronize soldiers

blocks.note: first meaning: customers who frequent a pub or shop
second meaning: professional troops of a standing army

clue.text: Nordic-looking IT novice makes bloomer

explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a crossword term for anything that blooms, and this woodland plant has bright blue flowers.

clue.text: Protein one German eats after every starter?

whoever finishes behind all the starters in a race comes last

clue.text: Delivery of Congressional results?

clue.text: You might say an eye and nose doctor enrages sons

explanation.definitionFit: Eyes and noses are examples of the bodily parts that detect sight and smell for the nervous system.

clue.text: Port and lemon a haberdasher holds

clue.text: Tail game by yard covered with stunted trees

clue.text: Writer everyone associates with black spot

clue.text: Sit on fence in a British spot

clue.text: Minerals found in choc-ice: salt, surprisingly

clue.text: What on earth is often called for these days?

J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: A judge growing accustomed to crime should step down.
explanation.walkthrough: Inuring takes a transitive sense, accustoming someone to hardship, so the definition reads 'getting used to'.
explanation.definitionFit: To inure is to accustom someone to something unpleasant so they no longer feel it.

clue.text: One hanging by door or heading to exit in anger

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter
something in another thing sits inside it

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
wrath is fierce anger

explanation.surface: Someone loiters by the door, or storms out in a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One hanging by door' suggests a lurking person, but it is a Christmas decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: A Christmas ring of holly or evergreens is traditionally hung on the front door.

clue.text: Pedant’s oddly dismissed worry

indicators.note: dismissing the odd positions keeps only the even ones

blocks.note: the even-numbered letters, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A fussy stickler has his strange fretting brushed aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like 'strangely', but it points at the odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat at someone is to trouble or bother them, as in asking what is eating you.

clue.text: Eighteen ornate fireworks out for doorstep delivery?

annotation.answer: WE THREE KINGS OF ORIENT ARE

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or awry, so the letters are disordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Eighteen elaborate fireworks are set out for a doorstep delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: Doorstep delivery suggests a parcel, but it is a carol sung by carollers at the door.
explanation.definitionFit: Carol singers go from house to house performing at front doors, so a carol is delivered on the doorstep.
